p: Because those are not prevailing wage contracts, we do not track the rates on that type of work.

Okay. What penalties or contract consequences does DPR use when a contractor provides false or misleading compliance information, and have those penalties been used on tree planting or tree maintenance contracts in recent years?

I'm happy to give kind of one response, and then look to our Assistant Commissioner for more information. But ultimately, we work very closely with City Law, with MOCS, with the Department of Investigations on all things related to any sort of infractions that are found to be with any sort of contractor. Really and truly, our bread and butter is making sure that this work gets done to New Yorkers, but we look heavily and work with our other partners here to ensure that there is compliance. And if there is an infraction, we are looking to those

other partner agencies to help us determine kind of consequences of that, and then follow up, as our Assistant Commissioner had referred to in sort of a monitorship in the situation that you had referenced earlier. I'm going to look to you, Ben, to see if there's anything else you'd like to add.

The only thing I'd like to add is that, you know, Parks contracting practices are not Parks alone. We're following the City's, you know, contracting rules, you know, in every way. So, when it comes to background checks, when it comes to compliance, you know, Parks contracting units, which, you know, I'm not a part of, do perform, you know, a certain background check, but then we do, you know, work with Law and DOI and MOCS for a more thorough vetting and compliance.

Final question from me, and I'm going to turn it over to Council Member Banks and Council Member Brewer. How concentrated is DPR's tree planting and tree maintenance work among its top vendors, including firms such as Dragonetti Brothers Landscaping and Griffins Landscaping? What percentage

of work is done by DPR's top three and top five vendors, and what is DPR doing to reduce over-reliance on a small number of vendors?

And while I'm going to look to our Assistant Commissioner to see if he has any of that information handy, I'm going to guess that we're going to have to get back to you on some of those other components of it. We have some data available here, but any questions that we don't have answers to, we're happy to get back to you on.

Yeah. I'm happy to kind of respond in somewhat general terms, which is that, you know, Dragonetti remains a significant vendor for both tree planting and tree maintenance and Griffins for tree maintenance. As we've discussed earlier, we've put a lot of effort into diversifying and recruiting more vendors, but we'll be happy to get back to you with the details on the breakdown of how much each of those vendors helps.
Okay. I appreciate that. I'm going to turn it over to Council Member Banks and Council Member Brewer.

Thank you, Chair. Just want to go back to some of my early questioning, particularly when it comes to Green Thumb responsibility and timelines, and also just want to note also that my District has the most Green Thumbs probably throughout the entire city. When it comes to trees inside a Green Thumb garden, when it comes to damage, when there's a property that's adjacent to it, when it comes to buckling of fences, cracked grounds, root pressure, which entity, Green Thumb or Parks Forestry is responsible for maintenance, and what is the required response timeline?

Sure. Yeah. I understand and appreciate that question, and of course, Green Thumb gardens are unique in that they're very close to people's homes in many cases. So, we are one Parks Department, so I wouldn't really characterize it as Green Thumb versus Forestry being responsible. However, Forestry takes care of the trees, right?
So, Forestry's responsible if there's damage that's done or if a tree's protruded onto private property.
So, Forestry can take action in terms of maintenance of the trees.
So, when a complaint is put in, what's the timeline for a response then?

So, we will inspect any service request as quickly as we can, and we discussed the volume and the backlog of service requests that we carry right now, so I can't provide a precise timeline for any particular service request. As far as --
So it could take two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, 10, 20 years?
To perform an inspection, no.

Well, but once it -- and this goes back to an issue of questions I had raised earlier, once inspection is done, and if we're not getting the response in a sense, or the rating that is needed to deal with the situation, who steps in when the constituent is saying and giving evidence

that their property's being damaged by this tree that is in the Green Thumb?

Yeah. So, let me just say, so what I believe that our Assistant Commissioner is trying to get at is that it really depends on the type of complaint that's coming in. Anything that is of significant, severe damage, or risk of damage, we are addressing as expeditiously as possible, and particularly, we have that rating system. But of course, we understand that there is a bit of backlog when it comes to those moderate and kind of middle-range complaints that are coming in, and certainly then, I don't want your constituents or frankly anybody to feel that they are just complaining into a void where there's no --
Well, that's what it seems like.

Right, and that's why I'm going to say that certainly we're an agency that's people-powered, so whether it's talking to our Green Thumb partners, which we do regularly, or it's talking to homeowners, or it's talking to our leadership at community boards or with you, Council Member, we are happy to walk through other

alternatives. We're happy to talk through what options are available and costs associated with it. So, I'd say we're happy to follow up with you directly to make sure that in this case that we lay out the options that are available, either that's, whether that's through Green Thumb taking action, Forestry taking action, or any other entity and what the timeline is.
We'll give you cases that exist.
Sure.

That it's already on the radar of Parks Department or the Forestry unit, and there's been no action, or not to the satisfactory of the need of the constituent, and it's particularly on Glenmore Avenue where you have a host of Green Thumbs that exists, and we have examples of damage being done to private property, and the resident has over and over said nothing's being done. So hopefully we wanted to highlight this today, and hopefully even get some action on that. When it comes to claims versus repairs, when a homeowner is directed to file a claim with the Comptroller for damages caused by Parks managed

trees, what documentation, inspection notes, findings, evidence of root intrusion, et cetera, does the Parks provide to support legitimate claims?
I'm happy to take that question, and thank you for that question. Okay. So, just a point of clarification, Parks would never direct a property owner to file a claim, but that certainly is an option.
But it is, okay.

Yes. And I would, to an extent, defer to the Comptroller as to what type of documentation they may accept or may recommend. However, Parks is happy to provide an assessment of the condition. Sometimes it's just simply a request for correspondence. We can write a letter saying, this is what we observed. When it comes to sidewalks, because it's a much more common type of concern, we have an established system. If a property owner is looking to undertake repair to their sidewalk, it's damaged by a City tree, they want guidance, or they are looking to file a claim with the Comptroller, or both, the inspection records that we provide a recommendation for a repair and

also documentation as far as what portion of the sidewalk is damaged by a tree.

Okay. And last question, Chair, and thank you. Does the Parks Department coordinate with DOT, DEP, Con Edison, National Grid, or other agencies when trees obstruct the street lights, contact structures, or create infrastructure risks? And I know this touches on, you know, in Brooklyn, we've been having a lot of brownouts and blackouts that has been taking place, and sometimes it starts either in a manhole, or it starts from, it's topical, starts from the lines, the electric lines. What is being done, is there any type of coordination?

Yes, very much so. On multiple different levels. So, on an agency-to-agency basis, we are in constant communication. We have regular interactions. On the staff level, we have regular interactions. And then during storms and during extreme weather events, we are even more so in truly constant communication through this kind of real-time task force that takes place that then helps us track using the resources of Emergency Management, DSNY, DOT, and others to

address and react and respond to situations as they arise. Would you like to add anything else to that?

Yeah. Specifically because you focused on brownouts, power concerns. I want to note that Con Edison is responsible for the clearance of trees, whether they're City trees or private trees, around their own infrastructure, but we have a very, very close relationship with Con Ed. We actually have applications where we share data back and forth. Con Edison refers conditions to us that they see may be a concern with respect to the health of the tree near their equipment. We refer conditions to them if we see something that is potentially putting their equipment at risk.
Okay. So, that's the coordination. Okay, got you. So, Con Edison is responsible for clearing.
Absolutely.
Okay. Thank you.

Some people may see trucks passing by, pruning around the wires, and then they may see our trucks passing by,

pruning for something different. They're on kind of distinct cycles. But yeah, Con Edison has a very specific cycle for pruning for clearance of their equipment.
All right. Thank you. Let's bring it back to Manhattan. Council Member Brewer.

Thank you very much. I saw the numbers for the tree risk issues, 34,000, and then sidewalk tree program, 17,000. But what's the backlog of trees to be planted? Do you have that number? In other words, an assessment maybe from your map or whatever, including the 47 that just died in the storm, et cetera, et cetera. How many trees have vacant pits in the City of New York?
Well, that number of trees that we could plant or plan to plant is a constantly evolving number.
Yeah. There might be a vault there. I got it.
Sure.
I know about the vaults.

Well, a vacant pit is not necessarily a planting space. Some trees may have been planted in tree beds decades ago in locations, whether there's a new conflict or just because our standards have evolved that space is no longer viable.
Okay.

In addition, we don't need a tree bed in order to plant. So, through our neighborhood tree planting approach, we're looking down an entire block. We are looking at every square inch of that block for where a tree could be planted based on our standards, whether there's an existing tree bed or not.

Okay. Is this on your map? I know you have a tree map, would that information be on the map? I'm trying to get a number to multiply 2,900. I'm trying to get a number so I can multiply it and figure out how much we need for our trees.
Okay. So, the Tree Work Hub shows our upcoming plantings.
Okay, but not where there are pits.
The question of how many trees could be planted in the entire city, I think that's what you're looking to get at.
Yes.
So, we have done an estimate, that would be an estimate. I don't have that number in front of me, but we would be happy to follow up.

Okay. What I'm trying to say is we all should be aiming for something for your tree planting program. Obviously more contractors would help, but you are talking about the most popular topic in New York City, so we would love to see some action on it.
And then just quickly, ma'am, I just want to interject and say that we have baseline capital funding in place for the tree planting program.
For all?
Specifically for the plan that we have designated.
Yeah. I don't like that plan.
Sure.
Okay. I'm just making it clear I don't like that plan.
But however, that end total, regardless of the timeline that it will take, the funding is in place.
Yeah. I need this parallel plan number. I'm working on my parallel plan.
Fair enough. We'll be happy to get you whatever information you need.

The other thing is just in terms of pickup for the recent storm. I know you said Sanitation and Parks, they'll figure it out. Will they figure it out at 3-1-1? I just worry when you say Parks and Sanitation, because I don't know who's going to do it. And I got people complaining, you know.
So, whether there's a storm or not -- COUNCIL MEMBER BREWER:Right.
-- the best way to report any problem with the tree is 3-1-1.
Okay.
That feeds directly into our database.
Into Parks? And then you decide if it's DSNY or you.

Yes. And when we activate the Downed Tree Task Force for a large storm through New York City Emergency Management, that pulls in multiple other agencies, depending on the conditions and what those other agencies are doing.
Okay.
And through NYCEM's Downed Tree Task Force, we feed work orders to other agencies who are coming in to help, and they feed their reports back to us, so it's a very tightly --

That's fabulous. And then, finally, what's that program called that you mentioned that you, because, you know, in my neighborhood, the trees bend the

sidewalk, people trip. Fine, they're still alive. But then the problem is then the neighbors, my neighbors, want to tear down the tree. I do not. So, what's the name of that program that could perhaps fix the problem so that I don't have to deal with tripping and I don't have to deal with tearing down the tree? Does it have a name, the one that you described?
The Parks' Trees and Sidewalks Program.
Parks' Trees and Sidewalks.
Trees and Sidewalks.
Thank you. I will be utilizing that program. Thank you very much.

I just want to take a point of privilege to say I want to be like Council Member Brewer when I grow up. So, I just want to say that. Going to the great Borough of Staten Island, Council Member Morano.
The Borough of Parks, Chairman. The Borough of Parks.
This is true.

Thank you very much, and thank you, Chairman, and congratulations for a very, very successful first Committee hearing. It's clear, based on the amount of preparation you've done today, that the Speaker made a great choice in selecting you to Chair this Committee. Congratulations as well to Council Member Banks for having the wisdom to ask questions before you figured out where the timer was. Commissioner, thank you not only for your testimony, but congratulations on a terrific appointment. It seems like the Mayor couldn't have chosen a better candidate than you. I'm really looking forward to hosting you in the Borough of Parks and showing you around some of the great parks in my District. Staten Island, as you may already know, has one of the highest levels of tree canopy in the city. Under the new data-driven planting strategy that prioritizes heat-vulnerable neighborhoods, can you assure Staten Islanders that we won't see reductions in tree maintenance, pruning, or stump removal services because our Borough already has a higher canopy?

Yes, I can. Our Tree Planting Plan is separate than our tree pruning plan. Those are two separate entities, even though we prioritize our heat-vulnerable neighborhoods, that does not mean we are leaving the rest of the city behind. This plan actually ensures that we are looking comprehensively across our city to make sure that everywhere is planted, but we also understand the importance, as mentioned in my testimony, of continued regular pruning. The continued maintenance of our tree canopy, of which Staten Island has a beautiful one, requires regular pruning, and we're very committed to following through on that. Would you like to add anything else about the pruning in Staten Island?

Certainly. So, yes, our routine pruning, our seven-year block pruning cycle continues. We continue to encourage Staten Islanders, along with all New Yorkers, to report any issues of concern that they see (INAUDIBLE) so that we can respond in between that cycle. I would add, with respect to Neighborhood Tree Planting, that we will be servicing, through that program, a portion of each community district. I

know Staten Island has three, on at least once in every three-year period, but also that that Neighborhood Tree Planting program is adding some capacity for tree and stump removal. We're able to use the capital dollars with our tree planting contracts to perform some additional removal of dead or dying trees and stumps as we go through and plant, so it's adding some service.

Thank you. And Commissioner, at the risk of being somewhat duplicative of what Council Member Brewer asked, I think it bears repeating, just because it's such a big issue in my District. A frequent complaint from homeowners in my District is the sidewalk damage caused by tree roots. Just to be clear, what steps is the Parks Department taking to reduce root damage to sidewalks when planting new trees?

Thank you for your question. And I'll look to Ben to give you more specifics, but as we've continued to maintain this urban trees that we have here, we've learned a lot of lessons and have evolved in what we understand to be the best practices around tree maintenance, and so whereas you used to see maybe smaller tree beds that

were maybe four by four in size, you won't see those anymore. You'll see these expanded tree beds that will allow for better root growth, healthier trees, and hopefully less destruction to our sidewalks. That's just one example, but I'll look to our Assistant Commissioner to give you more examples of how we've continued to evolve in our thinking of when we're planting new, that we're doing so with keeping in mind all the infrastructure that we're butting up against, but also the overall health and longevity of these trees.

Yeah. I would just add that we're even more thoughtful than we were in decades past about the species or cultivars of trees that we plant. We no longer plant trees that we've learned to be real repeat offenders with sidewalk issues, such as the Bradford Callery pears and certain types of maples, so just thinking about the species more carefully in this space.

I appreciate the update on the damage that the recent storms did to the trees. Does the Department proactively identify older or compromised trees that may be more likely to

fall during storms and maybe even remove them before they become a hazard?

While we are in the midst of our fourth tree census, which this year will include this sort of LiDAR technology that will be tracking the shape, growth, heights, type, of course, and all these other kind of details around each street tree, the truth is that all types of trees are unfortunately susceptible to extreme storms and extreme weather, so no, I don't believe, and I'll look to our Assistant Commissioner, we don't proactively go out to remove any of these trees or branches before a storm. We also, frankly, a lot of these times, these storms come pretty quickly, and the reason why we don't do any work during storms, of course, is that we have some really strict restrictions around putting guys in cherry pickers or anything else like that when extreme weather, this last one had gusts of up to 60 miles per hour winds. It would be way too much for our guys to go out there beforehand when these winds are starting to pick up and then do that work beforehand. I think our best approach is still that kind of regular interval of

tree pruning that happens on a seven-year basis. You want to add anything to that?

Just the seven-year pruning that the Commissioner referred to, it includes a full inspection of every tree on every block, so we have trained inspectors who are performing a risk assessment on each one of those trees, so those trees that are safe to remain at that time will be pruned under that routine maintenance, but those trees that are declining or have serious defects are given an even more thorough inspection and may be removed, so there is that kind of proactive inspection as we prepare for our block pruning. In between that cycle, we rely on the public to report defects.
One more, if I may, briefly, Chairman. When a new tree is planted for a block, how are residents notified, and is there any opportunity for homeowners to provide input about the location?

Sure. For our kind of comprehensive planting, your office should be notified as well as the community board about when

plantings are set to take place. You'll also see when the trees are actually put in, you'll see little tags on them saying I'm a new tree or something like that, and I believe that we're coming out with additional messaging to put on homeowners' doors and things like that to remind them that this is coming or that work is being done on their street. In terms of a selection of specific trees, unfortunately, we don't at this point. We're very limited in our ability to work directly with homeowners on maybe the type of tree or the location of these trees, because our mandate is really to plant in as many plantable locations as possible, and oftentimes, our decisions, as Council Member Brewer mentioned, are driven by things that nobody can see, the infrastructure beneath the ground, the kind of clearance with other sister agencies, and that sort of work. When I was Manhattan Borough Commissioner, I had residents who all they wanted were cherry trees in every location, and that's also not something that we can provide. We really look at the type of species of trees very closely to look at what are the other trees in the area, what can contribute to this kind of urban ecology that's going on in this space, what are the

trees that are likely to survive in the climate there, so a lot of those decisions ultimately guide, they're data-driven and research-driven, but they guide the decisions on where we plant trees and the type of trees that we plant, although we're also very happy, as I mentioned to Council Member Banks, I would love for your constituents to have a direct relationship with us. I want to hear their concerns and are able to explain these kind of concerns to our team, but also find ways that they can also be involved in caring for their trees on any given block or being involved with our agency in other ways.
Thanks very much.

Thank you. I just want to say, again, thank you to the Commissioner and the leadership at Parks and Administration for being here today. The goal of this Committee moving forward is to build a collaborative relationship so that not only are we protecting our trees, but our green spaces, our parks, our recreation spaces, and ensuring that every community has access to it, and so, again, thank you so much. As you know, our thing is parks are for everyone, so

we're going to do that together. Thank you, Commissioner. At this time, we're going to open the hearing for public testimony. I want to remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topics: Ensuring the Long-Term Health and Growth of the City's Tree Stock. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for

the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant-at-Arms. With that, we're going to call our first panel, and thank you so much for your patience with us today. Lynn Kelly, Executive Director of New York Restoration Project; Nisaya Price (phonetic), City Parks and Partnership for Parks; Sarah Balistreri, City Parks Foundation; Alia Soomro, New York League of Conservation Voters. And joining by way of Zoom, Kathy Park Price, New Yorkers for Parks. Lynn, you're good to start.

Thank you. Congratulations. I'm Lynn Bodnar Kelly. I'm the Executive Director of New York Restoration Project. I am no stranger to this table and delighted to be here again. I would say, as this is your first hearing, I would please encourage members of the Administration to stay and listen to the testimony of all of the advocates that have stayed in this room as we continue through this budget process. So, simply put, NYRP knows trees. For more than 30 years, we've planted trees, renovated

community gardens, restored parks, and expanded access to green space in our city. Together with the Parks Department, we actually launched and completed million trees, and this historic partnership was completed in 2015. As climate change intensifies, I think it's no secret, trees are our frontline way of defending ourselves and strengthening our biodiversity. And that's why today, and you can sign up on our website now, we give away free trees every year to New York City residents. This year, we're giving away 3,700 approximately trees. And I was told as of an hour ago, over 75 percent have already been claimed. So, get your tree now. We also do it in partnership with Council Members. We do a tree giveaway with Council Member Krishnan as well as Council Member Restler. So, next year, if you'd like to partner with us, you're welcome. I'm not going to go through why, because you're going to hear it from my colleagues about why tree canopy is so important in New York City, but I was doing some simple math while we were discussing the question about the nine years. Why does it take Parks Department nine years? Let's just do some simple math. If there are 18,000 inquiries or complaints or backlog on the books of

trees, and there are only 60 foresters, and the average U.S. worker works 250 days a year, that means that each of these foresters really has 1.1 a day that they would have to, and they can't get sick, and they can't take vacation. So, this is a function of resources. The Parks Department simply needs more resources. They're not miracle workers. Together with all of us (TIMER CHIME) as advocates, we wish to work with you in your new role. Congratulations, and you'll see me here again.
Thank you. Looking forward to working with you as well.

I just wanted to clarify, Nisaya Price from City Parks Foundation is my colleague, but she is not testifying in person today, and she was here, but is not present. So, I am Sarah Balistreri, the Urban Forest Program Senior Manager at Partnerships for Parks, a public-private partnership between Parks Department and City Parks Foundation. Thank you so much for calling this hearing and for the opportunity to testify. New York City has already taken an important step toward a greener future by passing

Local Laws 135 and 148, which established the Urban Forest Plan, and set a much-needed goal of equitably expanding tree canopy to 30 percent. In developing the Urban Forest Plan, City Parks Foundation has been partnering with New York City Parks and the Mayor's Office of Climate and Environmental Justice to plan community engagement, to use our extensive subject matter expertise to synthesize research and data analysis, and to act as fiscal sponsor for the Urban Forest Plan. Through Partnerships for Parks, we have coordinated large-scale community engagement efforts, including input sessions in all five boroughs where we heard New Yorkers' concerns and hopes for the future of New York City's urban forest. We also held focus groups with dedicated tree stewards and released a questionnaire which gathered thousands of responses in seven languages. To date, we've engaged more than 8,000 New Yorkers across all five boroughs, and what we're hearing is clear. People care deeply about trees, and they know their neighborhoods best. That's why Partnerships for Parks is now translating community input into community action. We're incorporating support for tree stewardship throughout our programs, providing training, supplies,

grassroots grants, and networking opportunities to community volunteers who dedicate their time, effort, and passion to caring for our neighborhood trees. Community input and volunteerism are vital to this work, and Partnerships for Parks is proud to lead it. But without dedicated funding for implementation, the City relies heavily on advocates and volunteers to enact the plan. We cannot expand and protect our urban forest without investing in the workforce required to plant, maintain, and steward it, and New York City Parks is already chronically understaffed. We stand ready to partner with City leaders to turn this plan into sustainable action, but it will require increased funding, expanded staffing, and a long-term commitment to our City's trees and those who steward them. Thank you very much.
Thank you. Do you mind if I ask you a question?
Sure.
You mentioned trainings. Can you just tell me the type of trainings that are offered, and how can folks sign up?

Absolutely. Partnerships for Parks Technical Assistance Program

for many years has offered a variety of trainings to those who steward and activate our park spaces, and we're now expanding that to those who steward our street trees as well. There are workshops ranging from budget 101 to how to access grants if you're a grassroots group to even sort of group leadership development and hands-on stewardship skills. Those are just a few examples, and people could easily find them by Googling Partnerships for Parks and looking for the Partnerships Academy series. Open to everyone, free of charge.
Thank you.

Good afternoon. My name is Alia Soomro, and I'm the Deputy Director for New York City Policy at the New York League of Conservation Voters. Congratulations, and thank you, Chair Hankerson, as well as Members of the Parks Committee and for the opportunity to testify today. Our City's park system increases quality of life, promotes climate resilience, provides good union jobs, and fosters social and economic growth in every borough. As co-founders of the Play Fair for Parks Coalition, along with New Yorkers for Parks, DC 37, and over 400 organizations, NYLCV demands a City

budget that gives New York City's Parks the fair funding they deserve. NYLCV is also a member of the Forest for All New York City Coalition, and this is a coalition of over 140 organizations committed to protecting, maintaining, and expanding the City's urban forest. First and foremost, if we are to maintain and grow our City's park system, invest in our workforce, increase tree canopy, and prepare our open spaces for climate change, elected officials must increase the City's Parks budget. We appreciated that the Mayor promised to increase the Parks budget to 1 percent, but we were disappointed in the preliminary budget, and obviously, it's preliminary, so we are hoping that the City Council and the Admin by the adopted budget will increase the City's Parks budget. Right now, it's 0.5 percent of the City's budget. So, as we're going through the budget process, we believe that there is an opportunity to rebuild an agency that was crippled by decades of disinvestment, and more recently, four years of disproportionate PEGS cuts. Moreover, the City's urban forests and natural areas provide countless environmental and

social benefits to city residents. This includes reducing urban flooding, managing stormwater runoff, which keeps pollutants out of waterways, and very importantly, mitigating extreme heat, which impacts low-income and communities of color especially. So along with the Forest for All Coalition, we were a strong supporter of Local Law 148 of 2023, which the Council passed, requiring the City's first Urban Forest Plan so we're very excited to see this plan, and just wrapping up, we're very excited to work with the Council, the Admin, as well as Parks advocates here today to get the Parks Department the fair funding they deserve and see the urban forest grow. Thank you.
Thank you. Alia, I just want to say I was very disappointed with the preliminary budget as well so I share that sentiment. Lynn, do you mind if I call you Lynn?
Please.
I just want to go back to your testimony. You had mentioned that New Yorkers are able to request a tree. Where can they request?
You can go right now on your cell phone to our website, and it's on our landing page.
You mind just moving the mic up? I want them to hear this at home.

Yeah. If you would like to request a free tree, there are some rules. You have to plant it or use it in New York City. You have to be a New York City resident, but you can go right on our website. It's right on the homepage on the landing page, and you register right there. It's a really simple form, and we have many different varieties of native species, and I'm told today there's still pawpaws left, so you can get fruit trees, and all kinds of flowering trees, and blueberry bushes this year. We've expanded. We've went to bushes a little bit over trees, but it's incredibly popular program, and we give you all the instructions. If you've never planted a tree before, or you've never cared for a tree, we can show you how to do it, so novices are welcome.
Are folks limited to one?
Yes, because it's a hot commodity.
I know. I won't tell my grandmother. She'll get upset.

But next year, what I will say is, if you would like to host a free tree giveaway in your District, come to us early, and we can come out to you with the trees, work with a volunteer even, or other organizations in your District, and make sure that they get in your constituents' hands. And like I mentioned, Council Member Krishnan and Council Member Restler took us up on that this year.
Thank you.
You're welcome.
All right. We're going to jump to the Zoom room. Okay. Kathy Park Price. Hi, Kathy.

Hello, Council Member and Chair Hankerson, thank you so much to you and the Parks Committee for the opportunity to testify. Congratulations on your first hearing, and I appreciate your statements about the disappointment in the preliminary budget, and echo Alia Soomro's

comments as well. As you know, we'll be at the March 23rd preliminary budget hearing, rallying for a fully-funded parks budget in advance of the preliminary budget hearing. My name is Kathy Park Price, and I'm the Director of Advocacy and Policy at New Yorkers for Parks, a 118-year-old advocacy organization that fights for our high-quality, fully-funded parks and open spaces for every New Yorker. As Alia mentioned, we also help lead the Play Fair for Parks Coalition made up of more than 450 organizations across the city that support our park system. For many New Yorkers, trees are the part of the park system that we encounter most often in our daily lives, even if someone does not step into a park or plaza on any given day. As the Parks Commissioner noted during her testimony, trees are literally part of our City's infrastructure and need the same care and maintenance just like our streets, sidewalks, and sewers do. Tree-related issues are one of the most common reasons residents contact 3-1-1, and right now there are more than 30,000 unresolved service requests for tree care citywide. During the most recent winter storm alone, nearly 2,000
